prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing optical frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B024 as my single-part position after reading all eight round-1 statements and the chair's questions. The decisive point for me is that the lattice clock is a distinct physical idea, not an incremental step on earlier clock work. A magic-wavelength lattice makes the differential light shift of the clock transition vanish while many neutral atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, which gives both the statistical power and the freedom from Doppler and recoil shifts that neither a single trapped ion (2012) nor the comb as a frequency ruler (2005) provides. The consequence is a measured, independently reproduced result: systematic uncertainties near 10^-18 in several species and laboratories, intercontinental comparisons, tests of the constancy of constants and relativistic geodesy. That is the maturity test I apply, a stable observation checked by others, and B024 meets it more fully than any other shortlisted part. I do not rest this on the opening count; Mehlig and Lindroth are right that four first places do not substitute for the argument. On the chair's question about distinctness, I would put the distinction into the citation by naming magic-wavelength trapping. On the redefinition of the second, I treat it as a consequence of the discovery and not a prerequisite: the criterion is a demonstrated invention with lasting consequences, and a metrological body's timetable is not part of that test. On credit, I keep two names, Katori for the concept and first realization and Ye for taking the lattice clock to record accuracy and for the many-body, spin-polarized fermion clock work, which I regard as physics and not only engineering performance.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged in kind. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-ion prize sit close to this lineage, and a sceptical reader may call a lattice-clock prize a third award on the same ground, or an instrument achievement rather than a discovery, as Pearce notes. I think the physics answers that, but only if the citation is built on the lattice idea and not on clocks or time in general. Credit is also not airtight: Lemonde, Hollberg, Sterr, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock and national-laboratory groups made real contributions, and Olsson's question whether Ye is credited for co-invention or realization is fair; I read the supplied record as realization plus the many-body extension, not co-invention of the magic-wavelength idea. Finally, my own field is close to this one, so I may overweight how hard it is to reach 10^-18 and underweight how a condensed-matter or statistical-physics colleague sees the novelty. I have therefore tried to give B003 a fair hearing rather than defend B024 by field loyalty.

responses.point: Danielsson answers my round-1 maturity objection to B003 by pointing to high-temperature superconductors, where the observation was rewarded before the mechanism was known, and proposes a citation built on flat bands and correlated states without any statement on pairing.
responses.response: That is a fair precedent and it moves me somewhat. I accept that a prize does not require a settled pairing mechanism, and a citation limited to flat bands at the magic angle and correlated insulating and superconducting states would be defensible. It does not, however, change my ordering. In the cuprate case the observation was unambiguous; here several correlated phases still depend on twist-angle disorder and device quality, which other B003 supporters, Eriksson among them, also acknowledge. The three names omit the first experimental author and early confirming groups, and your own uncertainty list asks whether two names would be fairer. Because I cannot resolve those from the supplied record, I would rank B003 second and would not call it equally mature. I would be comfortable if a majority chose it with the citation you describe, and I would not read that as a scientific error.

responses.point: Mehlig asks me directly whether the many-body, spin-polarized clock work I credit to Ye belongs in the citation, since that determines whether the prize honours the lattice-clock invention alone or also the later precision programme.
responses.response: I would keep it out of the citation text but inside the credit rationale. The citation should name invention and realization of optical lattice clocks and magic-wavelength trapping, which is where Katori and Ye are the clearest originators. The Fermi-degenerate and many-body clock results are the reason Ye's contribution is physics and not engineering, so they support naming him, but writing them into the citation would widen it toward the whole precision programme and reopen the ion-clock and national-laboratory boundary that Johansson and I both want to avoid. On B006, I still cannot judge the Toner-Tu scaling tests from outside the field, and you concede that quantitative confirmation of the exponents is partial and that B024 is the stronger case if sharp measurable outcomes are the test. On that criterion we agree, and I read your candour as support for placing B006 below B024 and B003.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, flags that a metrology prize can be read as an instrument achievement and that B003 and B023 carry a stronger claim to opening a new field of physics, while noting that the redefinition of the second has not happened.
responses.response: I take the instrument objection seriously and do not think it can be dismissed. My answer is that a new physical regime is opened here as well: neutral atoms in a state-insensitive lattice reach a many-atom regime in which atom-atom interactions, lattice-induced shifts and gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample become measurable, which is physics and not only precision. I disagree gently that B023 is the better field-opener: after the 2016 prize a second topology award needs a strong case that the quantum spin Hall effect is a different discovery from the one recognised then, and I could not make that argument from the record. On the redefinition, I disagree that it is the formal consummation: the result is established and cross-checked, and a redefinition would be a consequence and not the proof.

responses.point: Olsson moved from B001 to B024 after the opening ballots and asks whether Ye is credited for co-invention or for realization to record accuracy, since the citation wording depends on it.
responses.response: I read it as realization and extension, not co-invention. Katori proposed magic-wavelength trapping and the lattice clock concept; Ye's group made strontium lattice clocks the record-accuracy standard and added the many-body and fermionic regime. I would therefore not word the citation as joint invention of the idea. The form 'for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks' assigns invention mainly to Katori and realization to both, and does not overclaim for either. I also welcome your point that overlap with enabling prizes is a framing problem: the citation should say magic-wavelength trapping explicitly so the distinction from the comb and the single-ion prizes is on the page. I would not move B001 into the configuration, since it has one supporter and the instrumentation boundary you mention is unresolved.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B003 first but calls B024 the best-attributed and most mature candidate and an acceptable choice, and observes that B003 is the widest common ground since six of eight members rank it in their top three.
responses.response: I agree that B003 is wide common ground and I am glad you grant that B024 is acceptable, since that makes the final choice between them a question of weighting and not of dispute over facts. We differ on weighting because I put more weight on a stable observation than on novelty of the phenomenon. On the two-name versus three-name question the chair raised, I do not think the clock and graphene cases are symmetric: B024's two names map to concept and realization, whereas B003 must exclude the first experimental author whichever of two or three names is chosen. That is an attribution cost I cannot quantify. I do not think wide second-place support should decide the question; if a majority leans to B003 I would ask that the citation avoid any pairing claim.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the magic-wavelength wording in the citation is enough to say so.
Whether Lemonde, Hollberg, Sterr, Ludlow, Hinkley or the ion-clock leaders have a claim strong enough to change the credited pair; the supplied credit does not settle it.
Whether the committee reads the pending redefinition of the second as a reason to wait; I do not, but others may.
Whether B003 will be judged mature enough if the pairing mechanism is left out of the citation, and whether two or three names fit that part; I cannot assess this from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: Disclosure restated and updated after the chair's question. During my doctoral period I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's frequency-comb prize is part of the boundary argument for B024. I also work in laser spectroscopy and coherent light-matter interactions, the tradition in which lattice clocks sit, and I have taken part in WACQT. I have no documented personal, institutional or collaborative tie to Katori or Ye, and the Hall stay was a training connection long ago. I do not believe it requires recusal, but I leave that to the committee, and I have tried to argue the distinction from the 2005 prize on the physics and not on loyalty. I have no tie to B003 or B006 beyond field proximity, and B014 (my second alternative) is atomic physics adjacent to my own field.
